```{r message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(randomForest)
library(lubridate)
library(corrplot)
library(readr)
```

I aim to predict the final ranking of the 2026/27 English Premier League season by estimating the home and away goals per match within the season in chronological order, outputting each team's goals scored and tabulating these results into a season ranking. I was motivated to predict goals rather than match outcomes after reading *(Goddard, 2004)* which described the increased information gain from predicting not only the outcome of the matches (win, loss, draw) but also the magnitude of the win or loss, as it gives a better indication of the strength of a team. We require that the match goal results be integers rather than probabilities or floating point numbers, and so I have decided as an initialisation to round any estimations to the nearest integer. I have decided to use a random forest method of predicting the goal outcomes of each match, and investigated whether they were suitable for predicting football goals and integer regression. The suitability of their use in football is justified by *(Schauberger et al, 2018)* where they use random forests for exact goal calculation in international football tournaments. Generalising this to the Premier League, I decided to instead predict a floating-point goal result and round it to the nearest integer, as this could give the model much more flexibility in prediction. I also expanded on their model by deciding to use two different random forests to distinguish between whether a team is playing home or away, training them to infer a possible advantage or disadvantage playing home or away. As a group, we agreed to train our models on data from the 2014/15 to 2024/25 seasons, testing on the 2025/26 season, and predicting the 2026/27 season final rankings.

I decided that in order to create my random forests I required two assumptions to drive the forecasts of my models: recent match data is more important than historical data, as a team's performance adjusts drastically compared to how it performs in previous matches let alone previous seasons, and so features must be weighted more towards recent data; secondly, intra-match data such as red cards, player injury, all independent and random events are difficult to forecast, whereas goal-related features are able to be calculated from historical goal data with more conviction. This is motivated by understanding what information is available to us before a match starts, and if we are predicting a season before it has happened it is difficult to know when these random events will take place, and since every match must have a result compared to red cards, this makes result data much more useful. Therefore, my features are entirely based on historical goal information with no dependency on non-goal match events. I also decided that instead of weighting features based on recency, I created rolling features which uses lagged match values such as the average goals in the last $k$ matches, where $k$ is our lag value. We will see below how varying $k$ affects how well our model predicts. This is motivated by *(Dixon et al, 1997)*, which evaluated the dynamical system of team evolution, and whilst they used Poisson modelling to describe the randomness of the system, I decided to use autoregressive lagging features from the last $k$ matches.  

In order to use these rolling features, I used a recursive forecasting method which uses forecasted match results to influence the prediction of subsequent future results, similar to the method I had researched in my Time Series Module *(Noad, 2025)* where we utilised Box-Jenkins $h$-step ahead forecasting. The Box-Jenkins $h$-step ahead forecasting method is usually used in time series data and so usually wouldn't be fitting for match outcomes, but we adapt it in this setting because the matches are in chronological order, and it is reasonable to assume the performance of a team from very recent matches is influential in their performance of subsequent matches. 

We use random forests as a way of reducing the variability that normal decision trees are known for by implementing bagging. Bagging, known as bootstrap aggregating, is a method where data is randomly resampled to form a new data sample with the option of duplicate values and is then classified upon. After completing this with $m$ bootstraps in parallel, we average the results in the aggregating step to create a final outcome. In a random forest, we use decision trees as the classifier, however instead of using all features at the splitting step where we choose the feature that provides the best outcome of the tree under our chosen loss function, we use a random subset of features from which to choose the split with the lowest error. Choosing from a random subset makes the decision trees less similar, which allows us to observe which features are most important in creating the strongest tree, and using the squared loss function provides a stable final ranking of features for regression. 

An advantage of bagging is that it reduces variability, through the equation $$\text{Var}\bigg(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^Bh_b(x)\bigg) = \rho\sigma^2+\frac{(1-\rho)\sigma^2}{B}$$, where $B$ is the number of decision trees, $h_b(x)$ is the prediction made by decision tree $b$ of $x$, and $\sigma$ is the standard deviation and $\rho$ correlation of the tree's prediction. As the number of trees increases, the variance stabilises and even when correlation is present, the model regularises its fitting automatically by averaging many poor trees rather than using one very good tree since there is a higher chance of anomalies influencing a single tree.
